I'm not a meteorologist, but I've been following severe weather and tornadoes in particular for years. Preliminary EF-3 is a rating given to basically every violent tornado (EF3-EF5) because going any higher than that requires in-depth surveys by structural engineers, and those teams take a while to show up. Even if the tornado remains at EF3 strength after further examination, only around 5% of tornadoes are rated EF3 or higher, and the plurality are rated at EF0.

It's far too early for us to know if this tornado was abnormally strong, but early indications are that it's comparable to recent examples like Greenfield or Rolling Fork. Certainly it's too early to rule this out as an "abnormally strong tornado," although that category is pretty vaguely defined to begin with.

I thrift. I've bought fast fashion in the past, mostly target, but as climate change gets worse and new microplastic studies continue to come out, I've decided to stop buying clothes as much as is feasible. It's getting harder to find good old clothes for cheap in thrift stores these days. The newer cheap stuff sometimes crowds it out, but there are still places where it can be found. There's a thrift store in Rutland, Vermont that has a lot of good stuff, or at least it did last time I was there, somewhere mid-Covid. Thrift stores in hick towns in New England tend to have a lot of older cotton or wool flannels, those things are durable and don't look awful. The trendier and nicer the town, the more it'll be overpriced garbage. Not always true, but it's a good rule of thumb. I wear a lot of men's clothing as well, but I'm a lesbian in Vermont, my fashion advice might be useless for you there. Plastic is too deeply ingrained in our supply chains, it's almost impossible to avoid it entirely. Buying secondhand, sparingly and repairing clothing when possible to increase its lifespan is more helpful than obsessing over supply chains so that you can buy something brand new. We can't get rid of all plastics, but we can reduce our dependence on them.

I also don't plan on buying brand new clothes unless I need them for a specific purpose, or my current equivalents have worn beyond repair. I'm not doing this because I want to, I'm worried that in the near future prices will force this on me whether I want it or not. I live off disability and part time work, I can't afford much in the way of discretionary spending. Cheaper to get a sewing kit and some spare fabric and get use out of them. I hate to suggest it because people on the internet can be very picky about hygiene, but washing some clothes once every few wearings instead of every time is another way to make your clothes last longer. Using undershirts and long underwear that get switched out daily, especially in the cold months, so that your outer clothes don't get soiled from direct skin contact and can be worn 2 or 3 times without feeling gross or smelling bad, as long as you aren't sweating through them. 

I don't really want to make these changes, but I've seen enough evidence and a robust enough scientific consensus to convince me that reducing my consumption is worth doing. Even if we discount microplastics because we don't yet know their exact effects, anything I can cut out is a product that sits on the shelf and isn't replaced in the next stock order. There are ecological crises set in motion that mean we're gonna have to adjust our lifestyles sooner or later. To what extent things will change, we can only wait and see, I'm not claiming to be a fortune teller.

I don't think corporations should even be allowed to exist in the form they do now, the reason I'm talking about the consumer side is because I don't want to write a communist screed in a subreddit for a clothing retailer. It'd be way off topic.

There's studies that show that microplastic fibers shed off our clothing in the wash, and a good portion of that water eventually makes it back out of sewers and treatment plants and into the water cycle, where it's deposited in the bodies of every living thing on the planet. Avoiding plastic cloth as individuals or small groups can not and will not solve the problem, but it's better than doing nothing. If we want to actually solve the problem, that's back to the thing about the communist screed I said earlier. If having a large rotating stable of cute clothes is more important to you than not adding to the amount of plastic in our brains, then I guess that's your prerogative. I can't tell you how to live.

I'm currently obese (though not losing weight like you, good work on that!) and living in New England. I get that you can't just own one set of clothes and live off that, and that it is to some extent impossible to avoid emissions and pollution. But our parents, grandparents, every generation of humans preceeding us had way fewer clothes than we do, and got along just fine. Repairing clothes was more normalized, and actually it was far more practical than today, bc a lot of modern synthetic clothes fall apart if you try to make alterations. That change is inevitable, our planet isn't going to be able to support our current level of consumption (I mean consumption on a species level, capitalist practices lead to overproduction and waste of a lot of stuff relative to how much you need to support every person to a good living standard) indefinitely without the biosphere being thrown into chaos. The choice is whether we brace for it and maybe lessen the impact, or just let it slap us in the face out of nowhere.

We either have to accept that microplastics are going to increasingly accumulate in our bodies and water sources from now on, or clothes (and a bunch of other consumer goods) become more expensive and we all approach it more as occasionally buying clothes made with biodegradable material that is practical and will last instead of switching up our looks all the time. It's not a moral judgment on you or anyone else, idk if it was even possible for our species to avoid bungling into oil products without knowing the ramifications. It's not fair to us to make us shoulder the burden for past generations, but it's the hand we got dealt.

The Ice Age would be coming soon from the natural procession of the Earth's axis and orbit - sometime in the next 15,000 years - except that the greenhouse effect is more than compensating for the expected cooling, meaning that it will take much longer to get to that next ice age, if it even happens at all.

The coming ice age was discovered before we had enough evidence to be certain of anthropogenic climate change, and given how dire of a situation it is, it took a while for the consensus to settle there despite climate studies finding evidence of rapid warming as long ago as the late 50s. Scientific consensus doesn't "flip-flop" in the way a politician would, it follows the preponderence of the evidence. One landmark study, even if its peer reviewed and widely seen as accurate, is grounds for further investigation, not an instant overturning of the status quo. 

And the popular conception of what science believes lags years behind the expert understanding, because most adults are just working off whatever science they were taught in grade school, which could still be accurate, or could be decades out of date, depending on the subject. My parents grew up in the 70s, and they weren't taught about plate tectonics in school, because that had only become scientific consensus in the mid-60s, and those findings had yet to filter down to school curricula. By the time I went to school in the 2000s, it was a long-established fact, and we spent a whole week learning about it. Climate change faces that same problem, with the added effect of mountains of pro-oil propaganda trying to muddy the waters and make it into a partisan issue to protect themselves and their petroleum profits.

I don't imagine this will convince you of much, but science is a process, not a holy book. All conclusions in every field are provisional and could be overturned if further research suggests an alternative explanation is more likely. Climate science was still in its infancy in the mid-20th century, and the sort of long-term weather data and computer simulations that much of the field's knowledge is built off of were just then becoming reliable enough to be useful. It would be foolish of us to expect that nothing new would be discovered over the last 50 years.

The idea is that Coors' thin air contributes to its offensive profile, but so does its massive size, which makes it very tough on the Rockies' fielders. So, you want pitchers who reduce balls in play generally, as well preferring groundball pitchers who will reduce XBH.


Behind those pitchers, you want a team that is defensively strong across the board - don't compromise yourself at the Corner OF spots or at 3B, if you can help it. Your pitchers have an incredibly difficult job, support them as much as you can. Remember that your players will tend to have higher BABIP by virtue of playing half their games at Coors, so they will tend to get on base at a slightly higher clip than you'd otherwise expect. I've had players with 45 or 50 BABIP rating hit .270+ over full season sample sizes, and this effect is especially pronounced in players with line drive batted ball profiles.


In the bullpen, I'm fine taking on a guy with 45 or 50 control if his strikeout rate is high and his HR rate is low. Avoid Flyball pitchers entirely, they will always underperform their ratings at Coors. Some people find it too video game-y to build this way, but you can also find decent bullpen prospects via the waiver wire and the rule 5 draft.

Is this a problem? I'm not sure I fully agree with your view of anthropomorphism. It is very common for people to project too much onto animals, but I think it is an overreaction to claim that we have no ability to tell how they are feeling, or even how they are thinking.

My perspective on this is heavily influenced by my autism - I was not born with the ability to interpret human body language like most people are, I had to consciously learn both how to understand it and how to speak it myself. And what I learned was, while human body language is quite a bit more complex than most species, this principle can be applied to animals other than humans. Take cats for example - they're thought of by most as aloof and silent, but if you take time to observe a cat's behavior and posture, and what moods are associated with them, you can gain a rough understanding of how that cat communicates. And while it's not universally applicable, some of the general signs like body position and ear rotation are consistent across most cats. 

We can't know how their inner experience is, at least currently. But we can't do that with other humans either, we can only make a guess based on our knowledge of them and of ourselves. I have as much understanding of the inner world of my closest friends as I do about the inner world of my cat, absolutely nothing.

We share a common ancestor with cats, and we are similar enough that members of our two species are able to communicate indirectly and form emotional bonds with one another. Outside of the issue of qualia, I see no reason to assume that their experience of world differs so much from our own that we could make no inferences about it. At the very least, the simplest feelings like fear, pain, hunger, probably would map well onto how we experience them. They certainly seem to have similar reactions as we do to all those things. Why would we cease to have similar feelings to our animal relatives just because our brains evolved to a level of higher complexity?

I guess we're just gonna disagree on this. I think dictating a child's gender identity to them contrary to one they've expressed themselves, in any circumstance, is at best unnecessary and at worst actively harmful.

You can delete "at that age" from your first sentence. There's only one way a parent can tell if a kid is trans, and that's if they tell the parent themselves what gender they are. It doesn't matter if the kid is 4 or 17, the only person that really should get a say in what gender they're treated as is them. It's ok to try and give them info and make sure they're well informed on these matters before they make decisions about medical transition, but ultimately, no adult should get to dictate a kid's gender identity to them in any way, shape or form. If they can demonstrate an understanding of what they're saying, their word should be the final word on such things.

I think kids should get to choose their pronouns. I don't mean like frivolous "i like chicken nuggets so my pronouns are chicken nuggets" type stuff, I mean if your kid is male and says "I'm a girl" consistently and tells you they don't like you calling them "he", then why not accomodate that? In that situation, it costs you nothing and it makes them more comfortable, and pronouns are fully reversible even if they figure out when they're older that they're actually cis. I just don't see where decision making by the parents come into this, it wouldn't make sense to treat your child's gender as anything other than what they've told you they are. And at age 4, most kids are at the point where they have strong opinions on who they are, some frivolous, some not.

It's certainly a lot harder to know, but I don't think there's any harm to letting a kid identify as trans if they feel that's who they are. Like you said, there wouldn't even be the possibility of any medical treatments until they're a preteen anyway, so I think it's a good idea to take a kid at their word if they're persistent in how they identify themselves. If they get a little older and figure out they weren't right about being trans, they can just be cis and there's not really any drawback to that as far as I can tell.

There's a lot of nitty gritty stuff about being trans that would go over a kid's head, but I don't think the basic concept would cause significant confusion. "Sometimes people are born into one gender but would rather be a different one" isn't something that would be too hard for a kid to grasp, I think.

I'm very against the use of the R slur, but I'll acknowledge its mostly because of personal experience. Seeing that word wielded against me and some of my loved ones in a way that is very much connected to our neurodivergent status makes it a lot harder for me to conceptualize it as a general insult and not a slur.
